assumptions: Slot values range over {0,...,7}, so the outer mod 8 never fires
The loader is XOR with the fixed mask 3
conventions: XOR with a constant mask toggles exactly the bits set in the mask
The loader is realized by two X gates on the two low wires
question: A reversible source-loader on three little-endian bits is defined by the rule that maps each slot value s in {0,...,7} to (s XOR 3) mod 8, i.e. it flips the two low-order bits of s. Prove that this loader is its own inverse (an involution) as a permutation of {0,...,7}, and give the explicit image list obtained by applying it to 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 in order. Explain why the involution property is exactly what lets the two bit-flip gates that realize it also undo it when applied a second time.

assumptions: The work wire is a reusable scratch wire borrowed by the modular adder
The clean-action contract is asserted only under the hypothesis work=0
conventions: Wire order is address[0..2], row[0..2], work
The clean branch is the subspace where the work wire enters at 0
question: A fixed seven-wire reversible access circuit stores an address word on wires 0-2, a row word on wires 3-5, and one reusable work wire 6. On any input whose work wire is already 0, the circuit outputs the address word replaced by (loader(address)+row) mod 8, leaves the row word unchanged, and returns the work wire to 0. State precisely why the hypothesis 'work wire starts at 0' is required rather than cosmetic, what three separate guarantees the clean-branch contract bundles, and what can fail if the circuit is run on an input whose work wire starts at 1.

assumptions: The reversible program induces a bijection of basis strings
The compiled matrix is the ordered product of emitted primitive-gate matrices
conventions: The permutation matrix sends column c to the single row E(c)
Compilation is a separate pipeline from the combinatorial bijection
question: A reversible program on seven wires induces a bijection of the 2^7 computational-basis strings. Two objects are then formed: the permutation matrix of that bijection (the 0/1 matrix with a single 1 in each row and column recording where each basis string is sent), and the matrix obtained by compiling the program into a primitive gate list and multiplying the primitive gate matrices in order. Prove that these two matrices are equal, and explain why this 'compile-then-evaluate equals evaluate-the-bijection' statement is a refinement guarantee rather than a definition, and why it forces the compiled matrix to be a 0/1 permutation matrix.

assumptions: c and s are real scalars embedded in the complex field
Unitarity means the conjugate transpose times the matrix equals the identity
conventions: The matrix has top row (c,-s) and bottom row (s,c)
Conjugation is the identity on real entries
question: A real planar rotation embedded over the complex numbers is the 2x2 matrix with top row (c, -s) and bottom row (s, c) for real scalars c and s. Prove that this matrix is unitary exactly when c^2 + s^2 = 1, by computing all four entries of the product of its conjugate transpose with itself, and explain why no further hypothesis on c and s is needed and why complex conjugation plays no role here.

assumptions: The angle t(x) satisfies cos t(x) = x on -1 <= x <= 1 and is extended in some unspecified way elsewhere
The clean entry is read as the top-left matrix element
conventions: The amplitude gate is the planar rotation through an inverse-cosine branch of x
The cosine of any real angle lies in the closed interval [-1, 1]
question: An amplitude-loading gate is built from a planar rotation through an angle t(x), where t is any fixed real-valued function of the real parameter x chosen so that on the interval -1 <= x <= 1 the cosine of t(x) equals x (an inverse-cosine branch), and extended in some unspecified way to the rest of the real line. Two claims are on the table: (A) the gate is unitary for every real x, with no restriction and independent of how t is extended; (B) the top-left entry of the gate equals x. Decide for which values of x each claim holds. Prove the unconditional claim, prove that claim (B) holds for -1 <= x <= 1, and prove that claim (B) FAILS whenever |x| > 1 without using any particular value of the extension. Explain the asymmetry: why unitarity is free but the clean-entry readout needs -1 <= x <= 1.

assumptions: Each diagonal block B_k is unitary on the shared target space
The full operator is block-diagonal in the control index
conventions: Off-diagonal blocks of a block-diagonal matrix are zero
Unitarity means the conjugate transpose times the operator is the identity
question: A controlled family of operators is placed block-diagonally: for each control value k there is a block B_k acting on the same target space, and the full operator is the block-diagonal matrix whose k-th diagonal block is B_k. Prove that if every block B_k is unitary then the whole block-diagonal operator is unitary, by showing how the conjugate transpose interacts with the block-diagonal structure and that the product collapses block-by-block to the identity.

assumptions: The operator O is unitary before relabelling
Rows and columns are reindexed by one and the same bijection
conventions: Reindexing is an algebra equivalence, hence multiplicative
The identity matrix reindexes to the identity
question: Suppose an operator on a finite register is unitary, and we relabel the register's basis by a bijection (reindexing both rows and columns through the same equivalence of index sets). Prove that the reindexed operator is again unitary. Make explicit how the conjugate transpose commutes with reindexing and why using the SAME equivalence on rows and columns is essential for the argument to close.

assumptions: PREPARE is unitary on the selector register alone
The lift tensors identities on the coefficient and system registers
conventions: The identity matrix is a unitary on any register
star of a Kronecker product is the Kronecker product of the stars
question: A state-preparation unitary acts only on a selector register, but inside a composite machine it is applied on the full product register coefficient x (selector x system) as identity-on-coefficient tensor (PREPARE tensor identity-on-system). Prove that if PREPARE is unitary on the selector register alone then this tensor-lifted operator is unitary on the whole product register, and explain the physical reading: tensoring a gate with 'do nothing' on untouched registers never spoils unitarity.

assumptions: Each selector value s names a permutation p_s of the system register
SELECT preserves the coefficient and selector registers
conventions: The forward map carries the selector through unchanged
A basis permutation's matrix is a 0/1 permutation matrix
question: A coherently controlled SELECT applies, for each selector value s, a permutation p_s of the system register, while leaving the coefficient and selector registers fixed. Prove that the map sending (coeff, (s, x)) to (coeff, (s, p_s(x))) is a genuine bijection of the whole product register by exhibiting its two-sided inverse, and explain why its matrix is automatically unitary. Why is it essential that the inverse applies the inverse permutation (p_s)^{-1} indexed by the SAME selector value s that is read on input?

assumptions: Each permutation matrix has exactly one 1 per row and per column
Matrices act on column vectors by left multiplication
conventions: P(e)[r,c] = 1 iff r = e(c)
The composite 'first then second' sends c to second(first(c))
question: Finite basis permutations are represented by 0/1 matrices: for a bijection e of the index set, its matrix has a 1 at (row, column) exactly when row = e(column). Prove that composing two such permutation matrices multiplies them in reverse order: the matrix of the composite that does 'first then second' equals (matrix of second) times (matrix of first). Make explicit how matrix multiplication selects a single surviving term and why the order reversal is forced rather than a convention.

assumptions: PREPARE is unitary on the selector register
Every amplitude block is unitary on the coefficient register
SELECT is a basis permutation
conventions: The unprepare stage is the conjugate transpose of the prepare stage
Unitaries form a group closed under product and conjugate transpose
question: A logical block is assembled as PREPARE-dagger then SELECT then AMPLITUDE then PREPARE, applied on the product register coefficient x (selector x system). Prove that this whole composite is unitary, deriving it only from three local certificates: PREPARE unitary on the selector, every amplitude block unitary on the coefficient, and SELECT a basis permutation. State explicitly why the unprepare stage must be the conjugate transpose of the prepare stage and what role the group-closure of unitaries plays.

assumptions: The transcript is a list of named oracle-call labels, not matrices
Executable SWAP semantics live in a separate module
conventions: Effective signal qubits = declared signal qubits + visible workspace
The SWAP block is a paper label only in this adapter
question: A source-faithful adapter records a ten-block paper transcript as an ordered list of named oracle-call labels (preparation, an indicator oracle and its dagger, two difference-table oracles, a boundary rotation, a source-function oracle, a register SWAP that is a label only, and two closing daggers), and separately proves facts about register widths (system 3, signal 9, pure ancilla 6; total 13 physical qubits; effective signal 10). Explain what the transcript object does and does NOT assert about the circuit, why the SWAP being 'a label only' matters, and the distinction between the layout's 9 signal qubits and the effective 10 covered by the clean projection.

assumptions: The dagger is stored as the same matrix as the oracle
The oracle's integer image map is asserted self-inverse
conventions: A permutation matrix P is unitary with P-dagger = P^{-1}
An uncompute restores the register iff forward then inverse is the identity
question: A fixed indicator oracle and its stated dagger are certified for a warm Robin instance by four facts bundled together: the dagger's matrix equals the oracle's own matrix; the integer image map of the oracle is self-inverse; and the oracle matrix is a permutation (each row has a unique column with a 1, and each column a unique row). From these, explain the precise sense in which this indicator oracle is self-inverse, why 'dagger equals itself' plus 'image map self-inverse' together certify a clean uncompute, and what would break the uncompute if only the permutation property held without the self-inverse image.

Let (G, .) and (H, *) be groups with identities e_G and e_H, and let phi: G -> H be a group homomorphism, meaning phi(x.y) = phi(x)*phi(y) for all x, y in G. Prove from the homomorphism property alone (without assuming phi is injective, surjective, or that G or H is finite) that phi(e_G) = e_H and that phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1} for every g in G. State explicitly which group axioms (uniqueness of identity, uniqueness of inverses, cancellation) you invoke at each step, and explain why these two facts justify the standing claims that every representation phi satisfies phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}.

Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let <.|.> be any inner product on V. Define the averaged form <v|w>_G := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>. Prove that (a) <.|.>_G is again an inner product on V; (b) every phi(g) is unitary with respect to <.|.>_G, i.e. <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>_G = <v|w>_G; and (c) consequently, for any G-invariant subspace W, its orthogonal complement W^perp taken with respect to <.|.>_G is also G-invariant, so that V = W (+) W^perp as representations. Explain exactly where the ability to average over G is used.

Let (phi, V) be a representation of a finite group G over a field whose characteristic does not divide |G|, and let W be a G-invariant subspace with some (not necessarily invariant) projection P_W onto W (P_W^2 = P_W, im P_W = W). Define Q_W := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1}. Prove that Q_W commutes with every phi(g), that im Q_W = W and Q_W is a projection, and conclude that ker Q_W is a G-invariant complement, so V = W (+) ker Q_W as representations. Indicate where the hypothesis on the characteristic is used.

Let (phi_1, V_1) and (phi_2, V_2) be irreducible representations of a group G and let f: V_1 -> V_2 be G-equivariant, meaning f . phi_1(g) = phi_2(g) . f for all g in G. Prove that either f = 0 or f is an isomorphism (so V_1 ~ V_2). Your proof must show that ker f is a G-invariant subspace of V_1 and that im f is a G-invariant subspace of V_2, and then use irreducibility to force the conclusion.

Let (phi, V) be an irreducible representation of a group G on a finite-dimensional vector space V over an algebraically closed field F (for example F = C), and let f: V -> V be G-equivariant, i.e. f . phi(g) = phi(g) . f for all g. Prove that f = lambda . 1_V for some scalar lambda in F. Make explicit where algebraic closure and finite dimension are used, and derive as a corollary that any operator X commuting with an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity.

Let G be an abelian group. Prove that every complex irreducible representation (phi, V) of G is one-dimensional. You may use Schur's Lemma. Make clear exactly where commutativity of G and where the complex (algebraically closed) field are used, and explain why the statement can fail if the field is not algebraically closed.

Let rho be any single-qubit density matrix (a 2x2 positive semidefinite operator with trace 1). Using the fact that the Pauli operators {1, X, Y, Z} generate an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Pauli group acting on C^2, prove that (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z) = (1/2) 1. Base your argument on Schur's Lemma / the commutant-is-scalars corollary and on the trace, not on a brute-force coordinate computation.

Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional representation of a group G and define its character by chi(g) := tr(phi(g)). Prove that (a) chi is a class function, i.e. chi(h g h^{-1}) = chi(g) for all g, h in G, and (b) chi(e) = dim V. State precisely which properties of the trace and which property of phi you use, and explain why being a class function means chi is really a function on conjugacy classes.

Let G be a finite group and let the characters of its pairwise inequivalent complex irreducible representations W_1, ..., W_k be chi_1, ..., chi_k, orthonormal for the inner product (x, y) = (1/|G|) sum_{g} conj(x(g)) y(g); so (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij}. Let (phi, V) be an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex representation with isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_i W_i^{(+) n_i} (n_i the multiplicity of W_i). Prove that n_i = (chi_i, chi_V), where chi_V is the character of V. Then prove the two consequences: V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1, and two representations are isomorphic iff they have equal characters.

Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let ( phi_U, U) be a complex irreducible representation of G. Recall that Hom_G(U, V) is the space of intertwiners f: U -> V, i.e. linear maps satisfying f . phi_U(g) = phi(g) . f for all g, and that Hom_G is additive in each argument: Hom_G(X, Y (+) Z) ~ Hom_G(X, Y) (+) Hom_G(X, Z). Prove that dim Hom_G(U, V) equals the multiplicity k of U in the isotypical decomposition of V. You should use Schur's Lemma to evaluate Hom_G(U, U) and Hom_G(U, F) where F collects the irreducible summands of V inequivalent to U.

Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and for X in L(V) define the symmetrized operator Xbar := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that Xbar is G-invariant, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) for all h in G. (b) Using Schur's Lemma, prove that if V = W_1 (+) W_2 is a multiplicity-free decomposition into two inequivalent irreducibles, then in a basis adapted to W_1, W_2 the operator Xbar is block diagonal with each diagonal block a scalar multiple of the identity, and the off-diagonal blocks vanish. Explain which part of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks and which part scalarizes the diagonal blocks.

Let (phi, V) be a representation of a group G and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V with the swap operator F defined by F(|x> (x) |y>) = |y> (x) |x>, extended linearly. (a) Prove F^2 = 1 and that F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g. (b) Define Pi_sym := (1/2)(1 + F) and Pi_asym := (1/2)(1 - F). Prove that Pi_sym and Pi_asym are orthogonal projections with Pi_sym + Pi_asym = 1 and Pi_sym Pi_asym = 0, that their images are exactly the +1 and -1 eigenspaces of F, and that both images are G-invariant subspaces, giving V (x) V = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations.

Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G. For the trivial representation, define P := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g). Prove that (a) P is idempotent (P^2 = P), (b) im P = V^G := {|v> : phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g}, and (c) P commutes with every phi(h). Then explain, by taking the trace, why tr P equals the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V (the number of independent G-invariant vectors), connecting to the general character-projection formula P_W = (dim W / |G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g).

A student claims: for any representation (phi, V) of a finite group G and any X in L(V), the symmetrized operator Xbar = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1} is always block diagonal with respect to the isotypical decomposition AND each diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity. Decide whether the second half of this claim is true in general. Give an explicit counterexample using the action of S_2 = {e, (12)} on (C^2)^{(x)2} by permuting the two tensor factors (so phi((12)) = F, the swap), and explain precisely what feature of the decomposition makes the diagonal block fail to be scalar.

A student asserts: the tensor product of two irreducible representations of a group G is again irreducible. Show this is false by a counterexample. Specifically, take any representation (phi, V) of G with dim V >= 2 (you may take V irreducible) and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V. Exhibit a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V, and compute the dimensions to show V (x) V cannot be irreducible when dim V >= 2.

Proposition 3.22 says the decomposition of a representation into isotypical components is unique. A student over-reads this as: 'the decomposition of a representation into irreducible subrepresentations is unique.' Show by counterexample that the finer decomposition into individual irreducible subspaces is NOT unique, even though the isotypical components are. Use the trivial-isotypical component of the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} (equivalently, any space carrying the trivial representation with multiplicity >= 2) and exhibit two genuinely different splittings into irreducible lines.

A student claims: 'every finite-dimensional representation of every group can be made unitary by averaging an inner product over the group, so every invariant subspace has an invariant complement.' Explain why the averaging argument requires the group to be finite (or compact, with Haar measure), and give a counterexample: a finite-dimensional representation of an infinite group that has an invariant subspace with NO invariant complement (hence is not unitarizable and not completely reducible).

Part (ii) of Schur's Lemma concludes that a G-equivariant endomorphism of an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity, under the hypothesis that the field is algebraically closed. Delineate the boundary of this result: show precisely why algebraic closure is needed by exhibiting an irreducible real representation whose equivariant endomorphism algebra (commutant) is strictly larger than the real scalars, and state what part (i) still guarantees without algebraic closure.

Many representation-theoretic results for finite groups (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthogonality) are proved using the averaging (1/|G|) sum_{g in G}. For compact groups this is replaced by integration against the Haar probability measure. Delineate carefully which statements carry over verbatim to infinite compact groups and which must be modified or fail. In particular address: (a) existence of invariant complements and complete reducibility; (b) finite-dimensionality of irreducible representations; (c) the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and formulas explicitly involving |G|.

For a finite-dimensional representation (phi, V) of a group G, the dual representation (phi^*, V^*) is defined by phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that in a basis phi^*(g) = phi(g^{-1})^T, and that if (phi, V) is unitary then phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)) (the entrywise complex conjugate). (b) Delineate the boundary between a representation and its dual: give the character relation chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations, and explain precisely when V is isomorphic to its dual (self-dual) versus not, giving an explicit example of a NON-self-dual irreducible representation. (c) State what remains true regardless: (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is.

assumptions: Each U_i is a (beta,a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i) with common a and common beta
The output register is prepared in the exact uniform superposition over 2^m labels
|psi> is a normalized pure system state
conventions: sqrt(P_i) denotes the unique positive semidefinite square root of the PSD effect P_i
Postselection on 0^a means projecting the ancilla onto |0^a> and renormalizing
question: A POVM P = {P_i : i in [2^m]} is implemented through block encodings as follows. For each outcome i we are given a unitary U_i that is a (beta, a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i), all sharing the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta > 0, so that U_i |0^a> |psi> = (1/beta) |0^a> sqrt(P_i) |psi> + |perp_i>, where (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Define the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i acting on an output register in the uniform superposition |u> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i>, an ancilla register |0^a>, and the system register |psi>. After applying W one measures the ancilla register and postselects on the outcome 0^a. Starting from |u> |0^a> |psi>, derive in full the probability P(succ) of obtaining 0^a on the ancilla, show that it equals exactly 1/(beta^2 2^m) independent of the input state |psi>, and identify precisely where the POVM completeness relation sum_i P_i = I and the mutual orthogonality of the output-register basis states are used.

assumptions: Postselection on 0^a has already succeeded
The |i> form an orthonormal computational basis of the output register
P_i are PSD effects summing to the identity
conventions: sqrt(P_i) is the unique PSD square root
Mixed-state results are obtained by convex-linear extension of the pure-state map
question: Continue the POVM-by-block-encoding construction of Lemma 9.15: after applying W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i to |u> |0^a> |psi> and successfully postselecting the block-encoding ancilla on 0^a, the (renormalized) joint state of the output register and the system register is proportional to sum_i |i> tensor sqrt(P_i)|psi>. Prove that this joint state is correctly normalized, that measuring the output register in the computational basis yields outcome i with conditional probability P(i | succ) = <psi| P_i |psi>, and that the resulting post-measurement system state is sqrt(P_i)|psi> / sqrt(<psi|P_i|psi>). Then explain how the mixed-state update rule rho -> sqrt(P_i) rho sqrt(P_i) / Tr(P_i rho) follows from the pure-state result, and why the overall outcome probability for i (not conditioned on success) is still proportional to <psi|P_i|psi>.

assumptions: P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m) from the shared-beta block-encoding construction
A reflection about the good subspace (ancilla = 0^a) is available at O(1) query cost
The initial preparation uses O(1) queries to W
conventions: Query cost is measured in calls to W and W^dagger
delta is the target failure probability of the overall measurement
question: In the block-encoding implementation of a 2^m-outcome POVM via W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i (each U_i a (beta,a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i)), a single run succeeds (ancilla returns 0^a) with probability P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m). Explain quantitatively why naive repetition is wasteful, and show that amplitude amplification raises the success probability to a constant while using only O(beta 2^{m/2} log(1/delta)) queries to W and W^dagger to reach failure probability at most delta. State clearly which quantity plays the role of the 'good' amplitude, why the amplification cost scales as 1/sqrt(P(succ)), and where the logarithmic factor log(1/delta) comes from.

assumptions: 0 < |c| < 1 (states overlap but are distinct)
The ambient space is span{|psi>,|phi>}, two-dimensional
Unambiguity means a conclusive label never fires on the wrong state
conventions: |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are the normalized complements defined in the problem
A POVM must have PSD elements summing to I on the relevant space
question: Two normalized but possibly non-orthogonal pure states |psi> and |phi> are given with overlap c := <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and we are promised the unknown state is one of them. Consider the three-element POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, and P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where |psi_perp> := (|phi> - c|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) and |phi_perp> := (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2). Demonstrate by a concrete counterexample-style argument that NO two-element POVM {E_psi, E_phi} (with only the two conclusive labels and no inconclusive outcome) can be unambiguous, i.e. cannot simultaneously satisfy <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 while being a valid POVM, whenever 0 < |c| < 1. Then verify that the given three-element POVM is unambiguous and explain why introducing P_? is exactly the structural escape that restores validity.

assumptions: |c| < 1 and both states normalized
<phi|psi> = c*, <psi|phi> = c
conventions: |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are the unit complements from the text
Positivity of P_? is checked on span{|psi>,|phi>} since it acts as identity off that plane
question: For the unambiguous-discrimination POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where c = <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are defined as in the text, prove the three properties that make it a legitimate unambiguous POVM for state discrimination: (i) P_psi, P_phi, P_? are all positive semidefinite; (ii) P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I; (iii) the conclusive outcomes are unambiguous, i.e. <phi|P_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. For (i) you must actually verify that P_? >= 0, not merely assert it, by diagonalizing I - P_psi - P_phi on the two-dimensional space span{|psi>,|phi>}.

assumptions: W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i is the controlled block-encoding selector
Success is defined as the block-encoding ancilla returning 0^a
conventions: beta_i denotes a per-outcome subnormalization; a_i a per-outcome ancilla size
A valid POVM requires the implemented effects to sum to I
question: Lemma 9.15 assumes that for every outcome i the block encoding U_i of sqrt(P_i) uses the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta. Investigate what breaks if these two uniformity assumptions are dropped. Specifically: (a) if the U_i had different subnormalization factors beta_i, show that the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i followed by postselection on 0^a would NOT yield the clean superposition sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi> that is needed, and identify what spurious operator appears instead; (b) if the U_i used different ancilla registers (different sizes a_i, or disjoint ancillas), explain why a single joint postselection event '0^a' is no longer well defined and how this changes the success-probability bookkeeping. In each case state the minimal fix (if any) that restores the construction.

assumptions: ||A||_max < 1 and A_ij real so arccos(A_ij) is well defined and sin(pi theta~) >= 0
O'_A is a reversible classical-arithmetic unitary depending only on (i,j)
CR is controlled on the work register and acts on a single fresh ancilla qubit
conventions: A~_ij = cos(pi theta~_ij) is the d-bit-rounded entry
'Discarding' a register means tracing it out; a quantum computer cannot erase an entangled register for free
question: Given a real matrix A with ||A||_max < 1 and A_ij real, suppose we have a bit oracle that writes a d'-bit fixed-point representation of A_ij into a work register: O~_A |0^{d'}>|i>|j> = |A~_ij>|i>|j>. Using classical arithmetic one first produces O'_A |0^d>|i>|j> = |theta~_ij>|i>|j> with theta~_ij = arccos(A_ij)/pi in [0,1) a d-bit value. Then a controlled rotation CR transfers theta~_ij to the amplitude of a fresh ancilla qubit. Prove that the full procedure O_A = (I_1 tensor (O'_A)^{-1}) * CR * (I_1 tensor O'_A), acting on |0>|0^d>|i>|j>, produces exactly the amplitude-oracle state (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |0^d>|i>|j>, i.e. with the d-bit work register returned to |0^d>. State precisely why the final uncomputation step (O'_A)^{-1} is mandatory -- i.e. why the work register cannot simply be discarded ('no free cleanup') -- and what would go wrong with the amplitude oracle's action if it were left entangled.

assumptions: The amplitude is produced by a real controlled Y-rotation of angle 2 arccos(|A_ij|)
